progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: colourimetry against standards; matching a result to the right guideline and sample; gases are less soluble when warm; mg/L; dissolved ions conduct.
progression.startsWith: In late 1991, almost a thousand kilometres of the Barwon and Darling rivers turned green with cyanobacteria. In the summer of 2018 to 2019, near Menindee on the lower Darling, fish deaths were estimated at more than a million. Those deaths were linked to low flow, heat and algal blooms that left the water short of oxygen. So why would extra nutrients end in a fish kill, and what should chemists measure to see it coming?
progression.stopsAfter: tracing nitrate and phosphate from a source to a delayed oxygen crash; explaining why one look or one number can't judge water; choosing physical, chemical and biological parameters for a purpose and saying what each can't show; reading a nutrient and oxygen table to rank sites; stating why monitoring is needed (early warning, finding the source, judging against the right guideline, telling a treatment plant what to remove, checking a fix).

teaching.task: A river turns green. A few weeks later, fish are dying in it. Why would extra fertiliser end in a fish kill, and what should chemists measure to see it coming?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) nutrients are needed, and the scarce one holds growth back (2); (2) sources and point against diffuse (3); (3) feed and bloom; day and night oxygen (4); (4) die, decay, suffocate: bacteria use oxygen faster than it returns; delayed; warm still water worse (5); (5) memory aid and the word eutrophication (6); (6) one look isn't enough: three kinds of evidence (7); (7) physical (8); (8) chemical, including nitrate and phosphate methods (9); (9) biological (10); (10) worked read of the site table (11); (11) why monitor: guidelines depend on use; the source decides the fix; the treatment link; check the fix (12); attempts (13 to 16); handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: In late 1991, almost a thousand kilometres of the Barwon and Darling rivers turned green with cyanobacteria. Nitrogen and phosphorus aren't poisons. So where does the extra come from? After heavy rain, fertiliser washes off paddocks into creeks. With the brake off, algae multiply into a bloom, a green scum you can see from the bank. Then the bloom runs out of something, light or nutrients, and the algae die and sink. This chain is called eutrophication: nutrients enrich the water, too much grows, and the oxygen crashes. So how would you see this coming? Not by looking. Physical parameters come first. Chemical parameters include pH, dissolved oxygen and conductivity. Biological parameters look at living things. Let's read some data. So why monitor? A number only means something against a guideline for that water's use. Your turn. Nitrate, phosphate and E. Last one. One good set: water temperature, because warm, still water favours blooms. So, when you're asked why we monitor water, trace it from the source, through the bloom, to the oxygen crash, then choose evidence of all three kinds for the job.
teaching.openingDecision: In late 1991, almost a thousand kilometres of the Barwon and Darling rivers turned green with cyanobacteria. teaching.understandingCheck: - (A1) "A creek flows past a dairy farm. Water was sampled at three sites on the same morning. Site 1 is upstream of the farm. Site 2 is just below a drain from the dairy's milking shed. Site 3 is 5 km downstream, in a slow, shallow pool with green scum on the surface." Table (nutrients as the ion): Site 1: nitrate 0.40 mg/L, phosphate 0.03 mg/L, dissolved oxygen 8.6 mg/L, E. coli 40 per 100 mL; Site 2: 2.60, 0.42, 7.9, 2,400; Site 3: 1.10, 0.15, 3.2, 300. "(a) Identify the most likely source of the nutrients, using the data. (b) Explain why dissolved oxygen is lowest at Site 3, not at Site 2." Answer: (a) the dairy drain, between Sites 1 and 2, is the most likely source: nitrate rises about 6.5 times, phosphate 14 times, and E. coli 60 times there, and E. coli points to animal faecal waste; (b) nutrients take time to grow a bloom; the likely explanation is that at the slow, warm-looking pool the algae have grown, and as they die bacteria decompose them, using oxygen faster than the still water takes it back in; nutrients are lower at Site 3 partly because the algae took them up. Crossed mistake: "Oxygen should be lowest where the nutrients are highest" (the crash is delayed and happens where the bloom has grown and died). Differs from the site table in setting (a creek with a source between sites), the added E. coli column and the demand (locate the source; explain the delay). Not a copy of site Activity 2 (which asks least affected, most advanced, management).

scenes.visualReference: the board clears to the purpose card. Left: "drinking water" with a coded tap outline and a nitrate bar reaching a line "ADWG health value: 50 mg/L as NO₃⁻ (protects bottle-fed babies)"; right: "river ecosystem" with m8-lake-bloom-v1.png small and a much shorter bar labelled "far lower levels can feed a bloom" (grey tag "ANZG ecosystem trigger values; check the basis: as NO₃⁻ or as N"). On "Sampling above and below" the two coded bottles from scene 3 return either side of the outlet plate, with a step up in the nutrient tokens between them (tag "find the source → choose the fix"). On "treatment plant" a coded treatment-plant box outline appears at the right with two input arrows: from a dam outline "algae and toxins at the intake" and from the outlet "N and P in sewage" (tag "what to remove"; bright). On "recovered" a small coded trend line of phosphate over months steps down after a marker "fix" (tag "check the response"). Bright at the end: the treatment box tag and the trend line. Hold about 1 second.
scenes.teachingReason: So why monitor? A number only means something against a guideline for that water's use.
